insight.title: How a Simple Metal Box Built the Modern World
insight.subtitle: Why standardization is the hidden force behind global trade.

sections.text: Before standard shipping containers, moving goods was a slow and expensive mess. Workers carried sacks, barrels, and crates by hand onto ships. It took weeks to load a single vessel. This inefficiency made imported products incredibly expensive for normal people. Everything changed when a simple, uniform metal box was finally invented.

In the 1950s, a businessman named Malcolm McLean promoted a standard size for these boxes. Now, every container fits perfectly on a truck, a train, or a massive ship. Because every port uses the same locking system, machines do the heavy lifting. This allows for incredibly fast and reliable global loading.

Standardization collapsed the cost of shipping across the oceans. Today, it is cheaper to send a sweater across the globe than to mail it to a neighbor. This efficiency created the modern world. It allows businesses to build things anywhere, giving us easy access to affordable food, clothes, and technology.

news.title: PrEP uptake was already low - and then came the cuts
news.description: Even before the Trump government slashed its overseas HIV budget last year, with prevention facing some of the deepest cuts, very few countries in the world had enough people using PrEP to substantially reduce their HIV infection rate, or even to make a noticeable dent in it.
